idiom_name: Cell<bool> dirty bit with a RefCell<Option<T>> cache behind &self
implementation_notes: The borrow checker makes interior mutability the local idiom: the accessor takes &self, so a plain bool cannot be written there - the flag is a Cell<bool> (or Cell<f64> for the primary value) and the cache lives in a RefCell<Option<T>>, with get/set and borrow_mut as the primitives. OnceCell/OnceLock replace the pair for one-shot initialisation but cannot be invalidated (take() needs &mut self), so they serve lazy initialisation, not this pattern. The classic structure is still the right choice when several inputs feed one expensive value; a value with no mutation at all needs no cache.
pitfalls: Holding a RefCell borrow across the recomputation (which may call back into the same object) panics at runtime; copy the inputs out, drop the borrow, then rebuild.
Cell/RefCell make the type !Sync: sharing it across threads requires the atomic/mutex variants, and a CompileError names that directly.
OnceCell/OnceLock cannot be reset, and a panic in a lock's critical section poisons a Mutex - decide whether the cache should recover or propagate.
Clearing the flag before the cache is published leaves a permanently stale cache if the recomputation panics; set the flag false only after the write succeeds.

variants.name: AtomicBool flag with a Mutex-guarded cache
variants.idiom_name: AtomicBool dirty flag plus Mutex<Option<T>> rebuild
variants.implementation_notes: For shared objects the flag and the cache must be synchronized: an AtomicBool gives the acquire/release pair that a plain bool lacks (Rust's atomics follow the C++20 memory model and data races are undefined behaviour), and the rebuild runs under a Mutex/RwLock with a re-check so only one thread computes. The publication order is the contract - rebuild, store the new value, then clear the flag with a release store. The atomics module is explicit that it is for low-level synchronization and that higher-level primitives are usually preferable, so the atomic flag is the fast-path check while the mutex remains the source of truth for the value.
pitfalls: Data races are undefined behaviour in Rust: reading the cache outside the mutex while the flag says clean is exactly that, no matter how readable it looks.
Ordering choices matter: a Relaxed flag store can be reordered before the cache write, so use Release on the clear (and Acquire on the check) unless you can prove otherwise.
A poisoned Mutex (a panic inside the rebuild) makes every later access return Err; unwrapping propagates the poison forever - handle or recover deliberately.
Locking two mutexes (primary and cache) in different orders across methods deadlocks; keep a single lock or a documented order.
